stem:
2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is warmed in ethanol. The ether is the major product and the alkene is the minor product. How does the alkene form?
[[rxn:CCC(C)(C)Br>CH3CH2OH;>CCC(C)(C)OCC + CC=C(C)C]]

choices.h: {{E2}} mechanism with {{CH3CH2O-}} acting as the base
choices.why: No ethoxide was added. Neutral ethanol contains essentially no ethoxide, so this base is not in the flask.

choices.h: {{E2}} mechanism with {{CH3CH2OH}} acting as the base
choices.why: {{E2}} needs a strong base. Ethanol is a weak base and cannot pull the hydrogen off while the bromide is still attached.

choices.h: {{E1}} mechanism with {{CH3CH2O-}} acting as the base
choices.why: The mechanism is right but the base is not: there is no ethoxide in neutral ethanol.

choices.h: {{E1}} mechanism with {{CH3CH2OH}} acting as the base
choices.why: The tertiary bromide ionizes in the polar protic solvent. Ethanol, the only base present, then removes a hydrogen next to the positive carbon.

steps.h: The carbon that carries Br has three carbon groups: it is tertiary. {{SN2}} is impossible, so the choice is between a carbocation path and {{E2}}.

ask.q: Which mechanisms can a tertiary halide follow?
ask.a: SN1, E1 and E2, never SN2.

steps.t: List what is in the flask
steps.h: Only the alkyl bromide and ethanol. Ethanol is neutral: a weak base and a poor nucleophile. No strong base was added.

ask.a: No. Ethoxide is present only if a salt such as NaOCH2CH3 is added.

steps.h: {{E2}} needs a strong base because the base must take the hydrogen in the same step in which the leaving group leaves. A weak base cannot do that.

Ethanol is polar protic, so the C-Br bond ionizes to a tertiary carbocation. That one intermediate explains both products: ethanol adds to it (the ether, {{SN1}}) or ethanol removes a neighbouring hydrogen (the alkene, {{E1}}).

ask.q: What do the two products share?

steps.h: The alkene is the {{E1}} product, and the base is the neutral solvent, ethanol.

solution.answer: {{E1}} mechanism with ethanol acting as the base
solution.rule: Tertiary halide in a neutral protic solvent: carbocation, and the solvent is both the nucleophile (SN1) and the base (E1).

stem:
Bromocyclohexane is treated with sodium methoxide in methanol. Cyclohexene is the major product. Name the mechanism and the role of methoxide.
[[rxn:BrC1CCCCC1>NaOCH3;CH3OH>C1=CCCCC1]]

choices.why: {{SN2}} would give the ether, not an alkene. On a secondary carbon a strong base removes a hydrogen faster than it reaches the hindered carbon.
Secondary halide and a strong base: methoxide takes a hydrogen from the next carbon as bromide leaves, in one step.
This would be right with methanol alone. Methoxide is a strong base and reacts with the halide before it can ionize.
A strong base does not wait for a carbocation. With methoxide present the elimination is bimolecular: {{E2}}.

steps.h: The carbon that carries Br has two carbon groups: secondary. Every mechanism is possible here, so the reagent decides.

ask.q: What decides the mechanism for a secondary halide?
ask.a: The reagent (strong base or not), then the solvent.

steps.h: Sodium methoxide gives {{CH3O-}}. Its conjugate acid, methanol, has {{pKa}} 15.5, so methoxide is a strong base.

ask.q: How do you judge base strength?
ask.a: By the pKa of the conjugate acid: about 16 or above means a strong base.

steps.h: Secondary plus strong base gives {{E2}}, whichever solvent is used.
The product is an alkene, which confirms elimination. The hydrogen went to methoxide, which leaves as methanol.
Methoxide is the base. Methanol is only the solvent.

solution.rule: Secondary halide plus a strong base: E2.

stem:
1-Bromobutane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butyl alcohol. The major product is 1-butene. Name the mechanism and the role of tert-butoxide.
[[rxn:CCCCBr>KOC(CH3)3;(CH3)3COH>CCC=C]]

choices.why: A small strong base such as methoxide would do this to a primary halide. tert-Butoxide is too bulky to reach the carbon, and the product is an alkene, not an ether.
The bulky strong base cannot get to the carbon, but a hydrogen on the next carbon is on the outside of the molecule and easy to reach.
{{E1}} needs a carbocation, and a primary carbocation is too unstable to form.
No primary carbocation forms, and substitution would not give an alkene.

steps.h: The carbon that carries Br is primary. A primary carbocation never forms, so {{SN1}} and {{E1}} are out.

ask.q: Which two mechanisms are left for a primary halide?

steps.h: tert-Butoxide is a strong base ({{pKa}} of tert-butyl alcohol 17) and it is bulky: a poor nucleophile.

ask.q: Why is tert-butoxide a poor nucleophile?
ask.a: Three methyl groups crowd the oxygen, so it cannot reach the back of a carbon.

steps.h: Primary: a non-bulky strong base gives {{SN2}}, a bulky strong base gives {{E2}}. This base is bulky.
1-Butene is an elimination product. With sodium methoxide the same bromide gives butyl methyl ether by {{SN2}} instead.
tert-Butoxide is the base. It takes a hydrogen from carbon 2 as bromide leaves.

solution.rule: Primary halide: SN2, unless the strong base is bulky, then E2.

stem: Sort each reaction by the mechanism that forms the product shown.

items.why: Secondary halide, a weak base that is an excellent nucleophile ({{HS-}}, 126,000), polar aprotic solvent: substitution in one step.
Tertiary halide in water with no strong base: the carbocation forms and water adds to it.
The same carbocation, but water removes a neighbouring hydrogen. Heat raises the share of elimination.
Hydroxide is a strong base. It removes the hydrogen in the same step in which bromide leaves, and the alcohol is not formed.

steps.h: The first substrate is secondary. The other three are the same tertiary bromide, so for those the conditions alone decide.

ask.q: Can the tertiary bromide ever react by SN2?
ask.a: No. Three methyl groups block the back of the carbon.

steps.h: {{HS-}} is a weak base ({{pKa}} of {{H2S}} 10 in lecture) and a very good nucleophile. Water is a weak base and a poor nucleophile. {{HO-}} is a strong base.

ask.q: Which of the three is a strong base?

steps.h: In DMF, a polar aprotic solvent, {{HS-}} attacks the secondary carbon directly: {{SN2}}.
No strong base means the bromide ionizes first. Water then adds ({{SN1}}, the alcohol) or removes a hydrogen ({{E1}}, the alkene). Lower temperature favors {{SN1}}, high temperature favors {{E1}}.

ask.q: What do the SN1 and E1 products share?

steps.h: A strong base does not wait for ionization: {{E2}}. The lecture's rate law for this reaction is rate = k[t-BuBr][hydroxide].

solution.answer: NaSH in DMF: {{SN2}}. Water at 25 °C: {{SN1}}. Water with heat: {{E1}}. NaOH in water: {{E2}}.
solution.rule: Strong base means E2. No strong base on a tertiary carbon means the carbocation: SN1, and more E1 with heat.

stem:
A single enantiomer of 2-butyl tosylate is dissolved in water. The 2-butanol that forms is a racemic mixture. Name the mechanism and the role of water.
[[mol:CC[C@H](C)OS(=O)(=O)c1ccc(C)cc1|abbr]]

choices.why: {{SN2}} inverts: one enantiomer would give one enantiomer. A racemic product rules it out.
There is no hydroxide in neutral water, and {{SN2}} would give a single inverted enantiomer.
The secondary tosylate ionizes in the polar protic solvent. The planar carbocation is attacked by water on either face, which gives both enantiomers.
The mechanism is right, but the nucleophile is neutral water. No hydroxide was added.

steps.t: Classify the carbon and the leaving group
steps.h: The carbon is secondary, and tosylate is a good leaving group.

ask.q: Which mechanisms are open to a secondary substrate?
ask.a: All four, so the conditions decide.

steps.h: Water is the only other species: a poor nucleophile (relative rate 1), a weak base, and a polar protic solvent.
Secondary, polar protic solvent, weak base and poor nucleophile: {{SN1}} and {{E1}}.

ask.q: What would a strong base have given instead?

steps.h: A racemic product means a planar intermediate that can be attacked from either face: the carbocation of {{SN1}}. {{SN2}} would have given only the inverted enantiomer.

ask.q: What stereochemical result does SN2 give?
ask.a: Inversion: one enantiomer in, one enantiomer out.

steps.h: Water is the nucleophile. A second water molecule then removes the extra proton from oxygen.

solution.rule: Racemic product from one enantiomer: a planar carbocation, so SN1.

stem:
Name the mechanism and the role of {{HS-}}.
[[rxn:CI>NaSH;>CS]]

choices.why: A methyl carbon is wide open and {{HS-}} is an excellent nucleophile: one step, with inversion at carbon.
A methyl carbocation is unstable and never forms.
A methyl halide has no neighbouring carbon, so there is no hydrogen to remove and no alkene to make.
No carbocation and no neighbouring hydrogen: elimination is impossible for a methyl halide.

steps.h: Iodomethane is a methyl halide.
Methyl: {{SN2}}, always. No carbocation can form, and there is no hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon for an elimination.
{{HS-}} ends up bonded to carbon, so it is the nucleophile. Lecture rate law: rate = k[hydrosulfide][iodomethane].

solution.rule: Methyl halides do SN2 and nothing else.

stem:
tert-Butyl bromide is treated with NaOH in water. Name the mechanism and the role of hydroxide.
[[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br>NaOH;H2O>CC(C)=C]]

choices.why: This is what happens in water alone. With hydroxide present the alcohol is not formed: the strong base eliminates first.
A tertiary carbon cannot be attacked from the back: no {{SN2}}.
A strong base is present, and the rate depends on its concentration. That is {{E2}}, not {{E1}}.
Tertiary halide plus a strong base: hydroxide removes a hydrogen from a methyl group as bromide leaves.

steps.h: Tertiary: no {{SN2}}.
Hydroxide is a strong base ({{pKa}} of water 15.7).
Tertiary plus strong base: {{E2}}. The lecture measured rate = k[t-BuBr][hydroxide], and the product is the alkene, not the alcohol.

solution.rule: Tertiary halide plus a strong base: E2, even in water.

stem:
Name the mechanism and the role of cyanide.
[[rxn:CCCCCBr>NaCN;DMSO>CCCCCC#N]]

choices.why: Primary halide, good nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent: every condition on the lecture's {{SN2}} list.
A primary carbocation is too unstable to form, and DMSO is not a protic solvent.
Elimination would give an alkene. The product has a new C-C bond, so cyanide attacked carbon.
No primary carbocation forms, and the product is not an alkene.

steps.h: 1-Bromopentane is primary and unbranched: low sterics.
Cyanide is a good nucleophile and not a bulky base. DMSO is polar aprotic, the solvent type that favors {{SN2}}.
The nitrile has cyanide's carbon bonded where Br was: substitution, in one step.

solution.rule: SN2 wants low sterics, a good nucleophile, a good leaving group and a polar aprotic solvent.

stem:
tert-Butyl chloride in water gives tert-butyl alcohol as the major product. How does the alcohol form?
[[rxn:CC(C)(C)Cl>H2O;>CC(C)(C)O]]

choices.h: {{SN2}} mechanism with {{HO-}} acting as the nucleophile
choices.why: No hydroxide is present in neutral water, and a tertiary carbon cannot undergo {{SN2}}.

choices.h: {{SN2}} mechanism with {{H2O}} acting as the nucleophile
choices.why: The back of a tertiary carbon is blocked by three methyl groups: no {{SN2}}.

choices.h: {{SN1}} mechanism with {{HO-}} acting as the nucleophile
choices.why: The mechanism is right, but the nucleophile is neutral water. Hydroxide was not added.

choices.h: {{SN1}} mechanism with {{H2O}} acting as the nucleophile
choices.why: The chloride ionizes to the tert-butyl cation, water adds, and a second water removes the extra proton.

steps.h: Tertiary: {{SN2}} is impossible.

steps.t: List what is in the flask
steps.h: Only the chloride and water. Water is a poor nucleophile and a weak base, and it is polar protic.
Tertiary without a strong base: {{SN1}} and {{E1}}. The substitution product comes from {{SN1}}, with water as the nucleophile.

solution.answer: {{SN1}} mechanism with water acting as the nucleophile
solution.rule: In a solvolysis the neutral solvent is the nucleophile.

stem: Before choosing a mechanism you must know what kind of reagent you have. Sort each one.

items.why: {{pKa}} of water is 15.7: a strong base, and small.
{{pKa}} of ethanol is 15.9: a strong base, and not bulky.
{{pKa}} of tert-butyl alcohol is 17, and three methyl groups crowd the oxygen: a strong base and a poor nucleophile.
{{pKa}} of {{H2S}} is 10 in lecture, so a weak base, but the top of the nucleophile table: 126,000.
{{pKa}} of HI is -10: a very weak base. Nucleophile table: 80,000.
A weak base and a good nucleophile: 8,000 in the lecture table.
Neutral: relative rate 1 in the nucleophile table.
Neutral: relative rate 1 in the nucleophile table.

steps.h: A base is strong when its conjugate acid is weak: {{pKa}} about 16 or above for hydroxide and the alkoxides.
Among the strong bases only tert-butoxide is bulky. Bulk blocks attack on carbon and leaves only the removal of a hydrogen.
{{HS-}}, {{I-}} and {{N3-}} are thousands of times faster than water or methanol (1), yet they are weak bases.

solution.answer: Small strong bases: NaOH, ethoxide. Bulky strong base: tert-butoxide. Weak bases, good nucleophiles: NaSH, NaI, azide. Weak bases, poor nucleophiles: water, methanol.
solution.rule: Strong base: think E2. Good nucleophile and weak base: think SN2. Neutral solvent only: think SN1 and E1.

stem: Sort each solvent.

items.why: It has O-H bonds: a hydrogen-bond donor.
An alcohol: O-H, a hydrogen-bond donor.
An alcohol: O-H, a hydrogen-bond donor.
The O-H of the acid donates hydrogen bonds.
Polar S=O bond, but every hydrogen is on carbon: it cannot donate a hydrogen bond.
Polar, with no O-H or N-H bond.
Polar C=O bond, with no O-H or N-H bond.
Polar C≡N bond, with no O-H or N-H bond.

steps.h: A protic solvent has a hydrogen on oxygen or nitrogen that it can give to a hydrogen bond.
Water, the alcohols and acetic acid are protic. DMSO, DMF, acetone and acetonitrile are polar but have hydrogens only on carbon.
Polar protic solvents favor {{SN1}} and {{E1}}: they stabilize the ions formed in the slow step and solvate the nucleophile. Polar aprotic solvents favor {{SN2}}.

solution.answer: Protic: water, methanol, ethanol, acetic acid. Aprotic: DMSO, DMF, acetone, acetonitrile.
solution.rule: Protic means an O-H or N-H bond. Protic favors SN1 and E1, polar aprotic favors SN2.

stem:
Name the mechanism and the role of ethoxide.
[[rxn:CC(C)Br>NaOCH2CH3;CH3CH2OH>CC=C]]

choices.why: This is the minor path. It would give ethyl isopropyl ether, not propene.
Secondary halide and a strong base ({{pKa}} of ethanol 15.9): one-step elimination.
A strong base is present, so the halide reacts with it before it can ionize.
A substitution cannot give an alkene, and ethoxide reacts long before a secondary cation could form.

steps.h: 2-Bromopropane is secondary.
Ethoxide is a small strong base.
Secondary plus strong base: {{E2}}. Ethoxide takes a hydrogen from a methyl group as bromide leaves, and propene forms.

solution.rule: Secondary halide plus a strong base: E2.

stem:
Name the mechanism and the role of methoxide.
[[rxn:CC(C)(C)I>NaOCH3;CH3OH>CC(C)=C]]

choices.why: A tertiary carbon cannot undergo {{SN2}}. No ether forms from this pair.
Substitution would give an ether. Methoxide is a strong base and eliminates before the iodide ionizes.
This would describe methanol alone. With a strong base present the elimination is {{E2}}.
Tertiary halide plus a strong base: methoxide removes a hydrogen from a methyl group as iodide leaves.

steps.h: Tertiary: backside attack is blocked by three methyl groups.
Methoxide is a strong base ({{pKa}} of methanol 15.5).
Tertiary plus strong base: {{E2}}. The products are 2-methylpropene, methanol and iodide.

solution.rule: A tertiary halide never gives an ether with an alkoxide: it eliminates.

stem: Sort each reaction by the mechanism that forms the product shown.

items.why: A methyl halide has no hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon, so even a bulky strong base can only substitute.
Primary halide with a small strong base: substitution wins.
Primary halide with a bulky strong base: it cannot reach the carbon, so it removes a hydrogen.
Primary halide with a weak base that is an excellent nucleophile.

steps.h: One methyl and three primary halides. None can form a carbocation, so {{SN1}} and {{E1}} are out for all four.
A good nucleophile or a small strong base gives {{SN2}}. Only a bulky strong base gives {{E2}}.
Iodomethane has no neighbouring carbon and so no hydrogen to lose. tert-Butoxide has no choice: {{SN2}}, giving tert-butyl methyl ether.

solution.rule: Methyl and primary: SN2, except a primary halide with a bulky strong base, which gives E2.

stem:
Name the mechanism and the role of azide.
[[rxn:CCC(C)Br>NaN3;DMF>CCC(C)N=[N+]=[N-]]]

choices.why: Secondary halide, a weak base that is a good nucleophile (8,000), polar aprotic solvent: direct backside attack.
DMF is not protic, and a good anionic nucleophile attacks before a secondary halide can ionize.
Azide is a weak base. It attacks carbon instead of removing a hydrogen, and the product is not an alkene.
No carbocation forms in these conditions, and the product is a substitution product.

steps.h: 2-Bromobutane is secondary: the reagent and the solvent decide.
Azide is a weak base and a good nucleophile, not a strong base.
DMF is polar aprotic.
Secondary, aprotic solvent, weak base and fair nucleophile: {{SN2}}, with inversion at the carbon.

solution.rule: Secondary halide, weak base and good nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent: SN2.

stem:
3-Bromopentane is heated in ethanol with nothing else added. How does the alkene form?
[[rxn:CCC(Br)CC>CH3CH2OH;heat>CC=CCC]]

choices.why: No ethoxide was added, so this base is not in the flask.
{{E2}} needs a strong base. Neutral ethanol is a weak one.
Secondary halide in a polar protic solvent with only a weak base: it ionizes, and ethanol removes a hydrogen next to the positive carbon.
Bromide is an extremely weak base ({{pKa}} of HBr is -9). The solvent, present in huge excess, takes the proton.

steps.h: Secondary.
Only ethanol: polar protic, a weak base and a poor nucleophile.
Secondary, protic solvent, weak base and poor nucleophile: {{SN1}} and {{E1}} through the carbocation.
Heat favors elimination, so the alkene, the {{E1}} product, gains. Ethanol is the base.

solution.rule: No strong base means no E2. An alkene from a solvolysis is E1.

stem:
Potassium tert-butoxide is a bulky strong base, yet this reaction gives an ether. Name the mechanism and explain.
[[rxn:CI>KOC(CH3)3;>COC(C)(C)C]]

choices.h: {{E2}}, because a bulky strong base always eliminates
choices.why: Elimination needs a hydrogen on a carbon next to the one with the leaving group. Iodomethane has only one carbon.

choices.h: {{SN2}}, because a methyl carbon is unhindered and has no hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon to remove
choices.why: With elimination impossible and the carbon wide open, even a bulky alkoxide substitutes.

choices.h: {{SN1}}, because the product contains a tertiary carbon
choices.why: The tertiary carbon is in the nucleophile, not the electrophile. The carbon that loses iodide is methyl, and a methyl cation never forms.
A methyl carbocation is far too unstable to form.

steps.h: The leaving group, iodide, is on a methyl carbon. tert-Butoxide is the reagent.
A hydrogen on the carbon next to the leaving group. There is no such carbon in iodomethane.
Methyl: {{SN2}} only. The oxygen of tert-butoxide attacks the methyl carbon and iodide leaves. This is the good way to make tert-butyl methyl ether.

solution.rule: Classify the carbon that carries the leaving group, not the reagent.

stem:
tert-Butyl bromide in warm water gives both tert-butyl alcohol and 2-methylpropene. Which statement about water is correct?
[[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br>H2O;>CC(C)(C)O + CC(C)=C]]

choices.h: Water is the nucleophile in an {{SN2}} reaction and the base in an {{E2}} reaction
choices.why: Tertiary carbons do not undergo {{SN2}}, and water is too weak a base for {{E2}}.

choices.h: Water only dissolves the bromide. Hydroxide from the water does the chemistry
choices.why: Neutral water contains almost no hydroxide. The water molecule itself reacts.

choices.h: Water is the nucleophile toward the carbocation ({{SN1}}) and the base that removes a neighbouring hydrogen ({{E1}})
choices.why: One carbocation, two fates: water adds to it, or water takes a hydrogen from the carbon next to it.

choices.h: Water is the nucleophile ({{SN1}}), and bromide is the base that makes the alkene ({{E1}})
choices.why: Bromide is one of the weakest bases there is ({{pKa}} of HBr -9). Water, the solvent, takes the proton.

steps.h: Tertiary halide, no strong base, polar protic solvent: the carbocation path.
The C-Br bond breaks to give the tert-butyl cation and bromide. This step is slow and is shared by both products.
Water attacks the positive carbon: {{SN1}}, the alcohol. Or water removes a hydrogen from a methyl group: {{E1}}, the alkene.

solution.answer: Water is the nucleophile in the {{SN1}} path and the base in the {{E1}} path.
solution.rule: SN1 and E1 share one carbocation, and the solvent plays both roles.

stem:
Two reactions are shown. Give the role of each species.
Reaction 1: [[rxn:CI + [SH-].[Na+]>>CS + [Na+].[I-]]] Reaction 2: [[rxn:CC(C)Br + CC[O-].[Na+]>CH3CH2OH;>CC=C + CCO + [Na+].[Br-]]]

items.why: It ends up bonded to carbon: it gave its electron pair to carbon.
Its carbon is electron poor and accepts the electron pair.
It leaves with the electrons of the C-I bond.
It ends up as ethanol: it took a hydrogen, not a carbon.
It loses H and Br to become the alkene.
It leaves with the electrons of the C-Br bond.
It only balances the charge and is unchanged.

steps.h: Reaction 1: methyl halide with a good nucleophile, {{SN2}}. Reaction 2: secondary halide with a strong base, {{E2}}.
In reaction 1 the anion ends up bonded to carbon: a nucleophile. In reaction 2 the anion ends up bonded to hydrogen: a base.
The alkyl halide is the substrate in both, the halide ion is the leaving group, and sodium is a spectator.

solution.answer: {{HS-}} nucleophile; ethoxide base; the two alkyl halides are the substrates; iodide and bromide are leaving groups; {{Na+}} is a spectator.
solution.rule: Bonds to carbon: nucleophile. Takes a hydrogen: base.

stem:
Name the mechanism and the role of {{HS-}}.
[[rxn:ClC1CCCCC1>NaSH;DMF>SC1CCCCC1]]

choices.why: {{HS-}} is a weak base ({{pKa}} of {{H2S}} 10 in lecture), and the product is not an alkene.
DMF is aprotic and the nucleophile is excellent: it attacks before the chloride could ionize.
Secondary chloride, weak base and excellent nucleophile (126,000), polar aprotic solvent.
DMF is only the solvent. The sulfur in the product comes from {{HS-}}.

steps.h: Chlorocyclohexane is secondary.
{{HS-}}: weak base, top of the nucleophile table.
DMF is polar aprotic. Secondary, aprotic, weak base and good nucleophile: {{SN2}}.

solution.rule: A good nucleophile that is a weak base substitutes on a secondary carbon in a polar aprotic solvent.

stem: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is dissolved in ethanol with nothing else added. At 25 °C the ether is the main product. When the solution is heated, more alkene forms. Which mechanism gains from the heating, and what is the base?

choices.why: There is no ethoxide in neutral ethanol, at any temperature.
The same carbocation that gives the ether loses a proton to ethanol instead. High temperature favors this elimination.
A tertiary carbon cannot undergo {{SN2}}, and {{SN2}} does not make an alkene.
{{SN1}} makes the ether, the product that loses ground on heating.

steps.h: Tertiary halide in a neutral protic solvent: {{SN1}} and {{E1}} through one carbocation.
The ether is the {{SN1}} product, the alkene is the {{E1}} product.
{{SN1}} is favored at lower temperature and {{E1}} at high temperature, so heating raises the share of {{E1}}. Ethanol is the base.

solution.rule: High temperature favors elimination.

stem:
Name the mechanism and the role of acetate.
[[rxn:CC(C)Br>CH3CO2Na;DMSO>CC(C)OC(C)=O]]

choices.h: {{E2}}, with acetate as the base, because every anion is a strong base
choices.why: Acetate is a weak base: its conjugate acid has {{pKa}} 4. A negative charge alone does not make a strong base.
A weak base that is a fair nucleophile (630), a secondary halide and a polar aprotic solvent: it attacks carbon.
DMSO is aprotic, and the anionic nucleophile reacts before the secondary halide can ionize.
DMSO is the solvent only. The new C-O bond is to acetate.

steps.h: 2-Bromopropane is secondary.
Acetic acid has {{pKa}} 4, so acetate is a weak base, about twelve powers of ten weaker than ethoxide.
Secondary, polar aprotic solvent, weak base and fair nucleophile: {{SN2}}. The product is isopropyl acetate.

solution.rule: Judge base strength by the pKa of the conjugate acid, not by the charge.

stem: The same secondary bromide, four sets of conditions. Sort each reaction by the mechanism that forms the product shown.

items.why: A strong base is present: one-step elimination.
Weak base, fair nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent: substitution in one step.
Only a neutral protic solvent: the carbocation forms and ethanol adds to it.
Only a neutral protic solvent: the carbocation forms and ethanol removes a neighbouring hydrogen. Heat favors this.

steps.h: 2-Bromobutane is secondary, the one class where all four mechanisms are possible.
Ethoxide ({{pKa}} of ethanol 15.9) is a strong base: {{E2}}, whatever the solvent.
Acetate in DMSO: a fair nucleophile in an aprotic solvent, {{SN2}}. Ethanol alone: a poor nucleophile in a protic solvent, so the carbocation path.
From the carbocation, the ether is {{SN1}} and the alkene is {{E1}}. Both alkenes look the same on paper, so read the conditions: with ethoxide it is {{E2}}, with hot ethanol alone it is {{E1}}.

solution.rule: For a secondary halide: strong base, E2. Weak base and good nucleophile, aprotic: SN2. Neutral protic solvent: SN1 and E1.

stem:
1-Bromobutane is left in pure methanol at 25 °C. Butyl methyl ether forms slowly. Name the mechanism and the role of methanol.
[[rxn:CCCCBr>CH3OH;25 °C>CCCCOC]]

choices.h: {{SN1}}, with {{CH3OH}} as the nucleophile, because the solvent is polar protic and the nucleophile is weak
choices.why: The conditions look like {{SN1}}, but the substrate cannot do it: a primary carbocation never forms.
A primary halide can only substitute by {{SN2}}. Methanol is a poor nucleophile (relative rate 1), which is why the reaction is slow.
No methoxide was added. With NaOCH3 the same reaction would be much faster.
No primary carbocation forms, and the product is an ether, not an alkene.

steps.h: Primary. That removes {{SN1}} and {{E1}} before the conditions are even read.

steps.t: List what is in the flask
steps.h: Only methanol: neutral, a poor nucleophile.
Substitution on a primary carbon is {{SN2}}, with methanol as the nucleophile, followed by loss of a proton from oxygen.
Rate = k[RBr][nucleophile], and methanol is a far poorer nucleophile than methoxide.

solution.rule: The substrate comes first: primary and methyl carbons never use a carbocation.

stem:
1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane is treated with sodium hydride, NaH. Name the mechanism and the role of hydride.
[[rxn:CC1(Br)CCCCC1>NaH;>CC1=CCCCC1]]

choices.why: A tertiary carbon cannot be attacked from the back, and substitution would give methylcyclohexane, not an alkene.
Hydride is a strong base. It removes the hydrogen in the same step in which bromide leaves, without waiting for a carbocation.
Tertiary halide plus a strong base. Hydride takes a hydrogen next to the C-Br carbon and leaves as {{H2}}, while bromide leaves.
A cation has no electron pair to give. Sodium is a spectator.

steps.h: The carbon that carries Br has three carbon groups: tertiary.
NaH is {{Na+}} and {{H-}}. Hydride is a strong base.
Tertiary plus strong base: {{E2}}.
The products are the alkene, {{H2}} and NaBr.

solution.rule: NaH is a strong base: with a tertiary halide it gives E2.

stem:
1-Iodocyclohexene is stirred with NaSH in DMF. Which statement is correct?
[[mol:IC1=CCCCC1]]

choices.h: Fast {{SN2}}: iodide is an excellent leaving group and {{HS-}} is an excellent nucleophile
choices.why: Both are true, but the carbon is the problem. The iodine is on a double-bond carbon, and the lecture rate for vinyl is 0.

choices.h: {{SN1}}: the iodide ionizes and {{HS-}} adds to the carbocation
choices.why: A vinyl leaving group does not ionize: the lecture says no {{SN1}} for vinyl.

choices.h: No substitution by either mechanism: the leaving group is on a double-bond (vinyl) carbon
choices.why: No {{SN2}} and no {{SN1}} at a vinyl carbon, however good the nucleophile and leaving group.

choices.h: {{SN2}}, but slowly, as for any secondary halide
choices.why: The carbon is not an ordinary secondary carbon. It is part of a C=C, and substitution there does not happen at all.

steps.t: Look at the carbon before anything else
steps.h: The carbon that carries iodine is part of the double bond: a vinyl halide.
{{SN2}} relative rate for vinyl: 0. {{SN1}} for vinyl: no.
A good nucleophile and a good leaving group cannot rescue a carbon that will not react. Compare chlorocyclohexane, which does react with NaSH by {{SN2}}.

solution.answer: No substitution: a vinyl halide does neither {{SN1}} nor {{SN2}}.
solution.rule: Check that the leaving group is on an ordinary carbon, not a double-bond carbon.

stem:
(1-Bromoethyl)cyclobutane is warmed in ethanol. One of the products is an ether with a five-membered ring. What does that product tell you about the mechanism?
[[rxn:CC(Br)C1CCC1>CH3CH2OH;>CCOC1CCCC1C]]

choices.h: {{SN2}}, with ethanol as the nucleophile: backside attack opens the ring
choices.why: {{SN2}} puts the nucleophile exactly where the leaving group was. It cannot change the carbon skeleton.
There is no strong base for {{E2}}, and this would not enlarge the ring.

choices.h: {{SN1}}, with ethanol as the nucleophile: a carbocation formed and rearranged before ethanol added
choices.why: Only a carbocation rearranges. The cation next to the strained four-membered ring expands it to a cyclopentyl cation, and ethanol adds.
A carbocation is right, but the nucleophile is neutral ethanol. No ethoxide was added.

steps.h: Secondary halide, neutral protic solvent, weak base and poor nucleophile: the flowchart says {{SN1}} and {{E1}}.
The ring grew from four to five carbons. Rearrangement is the mark of a carbocation, so a concerted mechanism is ruled out.
Loss of bromide gives a secondary cation next to the ring. A ring bond moves to the positive carbon: the ring becomes five-membered and less strained.
Ethanol adds to the new cation and loses a proton: the ether.

solution.answer: {{SN1}}, with ethanol as the nucleophile, through a carbocation that rearranged.
solution.rule: A rearranged skeleton means a carbocation: SN1 or E1, never SN2 or E2.

stem: Sort each reaction by the mechanism that forms the product shown.

items.why: Tertiary chloride in neutral methanol: the cation forms and methanol adds.
The same cation loses a neighbouring hydrogen to methanol. Heat favors elimination.
Now a strong base is present: one-step elimination, no carbocation.
Secondary chloride, a very weak base that is a good nucleophile (80,000), polar aprotic solvent.

steps.h: Three reactions use a tertiary chloride, one uses a secondary chloride.

steps.t: Tertiary: is there a strong base?
steps.h: With methoxide: {{E2}}. With methanol alone: the carbocation, giving the ether by {{SN1}} and, with heat, the alkene by {{E1}}.
The alkene drawn is the same in two rows. The mechanism is read from the conditions: strong base means {{E2}}, neutral solvent means {{E1}}.
Iodide is a good nucleophile and a very weak base, and acetone is polar aprotic: {{SN2}}.

solution.rule: An alkene does not tell you E1 or E2. The base does: strong base E2, weak base E1.

stem: A single enantiomer of 2-iodobutane reacts in two ways. With {{NaN3}} in DMF it gives one enantiomer of the azide, with the opposite arrangement at the carbon. In water alone it gives racemic 2-butanol. Name the two mechanisms, in that order.

choices.why: Inversion with a good nucleophile in an aprotic solvent is {{SN2}}. Racemization in a protic solvent with a poor nucleophile is {{SN1}}.
This has the stereochemistry backwards: {{SN1}} racemizes and {{SN2}} inverts.

choices.h: {{SN2}} for both, because the substrate is the same
choices.why: A secondary substrate can follow either path. The nucleophile and the solvent choose, and a racemic product cannot come from {{SN2}}.

choices.h: {{SN1}} for both, because iodide is such a good leaving group
choices.why: A good leaving group helps both mechanisms. A single inverted enantiomer cannot come from a planar carbocation.

steps.h: Secondary: both substitution mechanisms are possible.

steps.t: Read the first set of conditions
steps.h: Azide is a weak base and a good nucleophile, DMF is polar aprotic: {{SN2}}. The stereochemistry agrees: inversion.
Water is a poor nucleophile and a polar protic solvent: {{SN1}}. The stereochemistry agrees: a planar carbocation is attacked on either face, so the product is racemic.

solution.answer: {{SN2}} with azide in DMF, {{SN1}} in water.
solution.rule: SN2 inverts, SN1 racemizes, and for a secondary carbon the nucleophile and solvent choose between them.
